Confucius. A Chinese philosopher and teacher whose ideas about proper conduct, family relationships, and social harmony fundamentally shaped East Asian civilization for over two thousand five hundred years. He lived from five hundred fifty-one to four hundred seventy-nine BCE during the Zhou Dynasty's decline, a period of social chaos that motivated his search for moral and social order. His name, Kongzi in Chinese, with Kong Qiu as his birth name, was Latinized as Confucius by Jesuit missionaries and he is often referred to as the Ultimate Sage in tradition. His teachings emphasize Li, propriety and ritual, Ren, humaneness and benevolence, Yi, righteousness, and Junzi, the cultivated person or gentleman, forming the foundation of virtuous living. The Analects, compiled by his disciples, are the primary source for his teachings and have been studied and revered across East Asia for millennia. He taught that moral cultivation begins with filial piety and extends through proper relationships: ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, and friend and friend. Confucius believed that good governance depends on virtuous rulers who serve as moral exemplars, rejecting the idea that rule depends solely on laws and punishments. His teachings profoundly influenced the civil service examination systems across China, Vietnam, Japan, and Korea, shaping their political and intellectual cultures for centuries.
